newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - WALL STREET JOURNAL - DEC 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - WALL STREET JOURNAL - DEC 16.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Monday's edition of The Wall Street Journal:
- Boeing agreed to acquire rival McDonnell Douglas for $13.3 billion in stock.
- Holiday sales are proving strong but retailers are concerned they have five fewer days than last year.
- Coca-Cola plans to introduce next month a citrus-flavored soda called Surge in what may be its biggest soft drink launch since Diet Coke.
- Delta called off discussions to acquire Continental .
- R.R. Donnelley plans to sell all or part of Stream, a software services company.
- WMX was ordered to pay $91.5 million to the original developers of the nation's largest hazardous waste dump.
- The U.S. and Japan resolved a trade dispute over insurance, with Tokyo conceding to U.S. demands.
- European Union leaders reached an agreement on measures to enforce fiscal discipline after the planned launch of monetary union in 1999.
- Bristol Hotel agreed to buy Bass's Holiday Inn Holdings in the U.S. for up to $670 million.
- Tobacco firms can be sued for alleged racketeering by Florida, a state judge ruled.
- President Clinton said parents should give an industry-developed television-ratings system a chance before trying to make changes in it.
- U.S. Surgical is set to lower its offer for Circon to $17 a share.

- Former Volkswagen executive Jose Ignacio Lopez de Arriortua and the German auto maker will face additional Justice Department scrutiny now that German prosecutors have indicted Lopez and three associates.
- Big Japanese investors say they plan to keep buying U.S. Treasuries, contrary to speculation that spurred a sell-off in U.S. markets last week.
- People are speculating about the real motive for Microsoft's convertible preferred share issue.

- While the stock and bond markets have taken roller coaster-type rides this month, amid a spike in interest rates, many economists and others agree that overall rates will remain relatively stable, at least for the foreseeable future.
